title: How America Built Entire Towns Just to Mine One Mountain
fullText: There is a photograph taken sometime around 1905 of a street in Creek, Colorado. On that street, you can see a five-story hotel, three competing banks, a department store, two newspapers, and a streetcar line running down the center of the road. Electric lights, brick facades, a population of close to 50,000 people living at 9,400 ft above sea [music] level in the Rocky Mountains. 20 years earlier, that same piece of ground was open wilderness with not a single permanent structure on it. 20 years after that photograph, the population had already started collapsing back toward nothing. The mountain underneath that city contained gold, and when that gold started running out, so did the people, the banks, the newspapers, the hotels, [music] and eventually the streetcar. This is the story of how America built entire towns, sometimes entire cities, around a single resource buried inside a single mountain. And more importantly, it is the story of what happened to the people who got left behind when the resource ran out and the company packed up and left. Because this was not an accident, it was a system, and that system shaped enormous stretches of the American West [music] in ways you can still see today if you know where to look. To understand how it worked, you have to [music] go back to the moment before any of these towns existed at all. In the mid-1800s, the American West was being opened up to settle at a pace that the federal government could barely manage. The Homestead Act of 1862 was supposed to put small farmers on the land, and in some places it did. But in the mountains of Colorado and Nevada and Arizona and Montana, farming was not what the land was good for. What the land was good for was ore. Gold in California [music] had already proven that a single discovery could move tens of thousands of people across a continent in a matter of months. The California Gold Rush of 1849 demonstrated something important about human behavior. Put word out that a mountain contains something valuable and people will appear seemingly from nowhere to pull that value out of the ground. The problem was infrastructure. A man could stake a placer claim and pan for gold in a stream with a few dollars worth of equipment, but the really valuable ore, the deep veins of gold and silver and copper that ran through the rock itself, required something different. It required machinery, capital, [music] engineering, and organized labor working in coordinated shifts around the clock. In other words, it required a company and a company working a mine at scale required somewhere for its workers to live. That is where the company town came from. Not from urban planning theory or civic idealism, from a very simple logistical problem. You have a mine in the middle of nowhere. You need 500 workers. Where do those workers sleep? The answer, in hundreds of cases across the American West [music] was that the company built them a place to sleep and then a place to eat and then a store where they could buy food and then a school for their children and then a hospital for when the mine injured them, which it did with remarkable [music] regularity. And before long, you had a town. Except, it was not really a town in the civic sense. It was a company asset. Every building on the land was owned by the corporation. The workers did [music] not own their homes. In many cases, they did not even get paid in regular currency. They got paid in scrip, a company issued voucher [music] that could only be spent at the company's store, which charged prices the company set, which ensured that a significant portion of every paycheck circled right back to the employer. The technical term for [music] this arrangement is a company town. The practical reality of it was something closer to [music] a controlled economy inside a fence. The company decided who lived there, what they could buy, how much they paid for it, and in some towns, what they were allowed to say in public about their working conditions. Now, this was not unique to mining. Textile mills in the South and steel towns in Pennsylvania ran similar systems, but mining towns in the American West took the model to an extreme that is still worth examining today because the scale of what got built and the speed at which it got abandoned has almost no parallel in American history. Creek is probably the most spectacular example. The mountain in question was the volcanic remnant called Mount Pisgah, sitting on the southwest slope of Pikes Peak in Colorado. In 1890, a cowboy named [music] Bob Womack had been telling people for years that there was gold in the cow pasture he worked on. Nobody believed [music] him. He had a reputation for drinking and for overly optimistic claims about the land. Then, in 1891, two experienced [music] prospectors named Winfield Scott Stratton and others began finding serious ore. Stratton himself staked a claim he called the Independence Mine on the 4th of July, 1891, and within a few years, he had pulled [music] out enough gold to make himself one of the wealthiest men in Colorado. Word got out fast. By 1893, the district had a railroad connection. [music] By 1895, the population had passed 10,000. By 1900, Creek and its neighboring settlement [music] of Victor together held somewhere between 40 and 50,000 people, making it one of the largest cities in Colorado at the time. The mines produced, over [music] the course of the district's peak years, something in the range of 800 million dollars worth of gold in the currency value of that era. Today, that number would translate to well over [music] $20 billion and the infrastructure that got built to support those mines was not rough or temporary. Creek had opera houses. It had multiple daily newspapers. It had electric street cars connecting the various camps and mines on the hillsides. It had a red light district that reportedly covered several city blocks. It had banks that financed operations as far away as Denver and Colorado Springs. [music] It was, in every meaningful sense, a real city. But the city existed because the mountain existed and the mountain's gold [music] was finite. The ore grades started declining in the early 1900s. Mines that had been pulling out high-grade ore at incredible [music] rates began hitting lower quality rock. The economics shifted. Smaller operations [music] started closing. Workers left to follow other strikes in other mountains. Then, a series of fires [music] in 1996 burned large portions of the town. Most of it was rebuilt, but the population never fully recovered. And when the deeper mines started flooding in the 1910s and '20s and the cost of pumping [music] water out exceeded the value of the ore coming up, the math stopped working. By 1920, Creek's population had dropped to around 5,000. [music] By mid-century, it was below 1,000. The opera [music] houses were gone. The street cars were gone. Most of the commercial buildings on Bennett Avenue [music] were empty or demolished. What had been one of Colorado's most significant cities had become, in the span of about 40 years, a near ghost town. If you are finding this video interesting, [music] now is a great time to subscribe. New documentaries like this one go up every week and and not want to miss them. Now, Creek story is dramatic, but it is not unique. Across the American West, the same pattern played out dozens and dozens of times. The discovery, [music] the rush, the company infrastructure, the boom, the decline, the abandonment. But some of these stories get even darker because some of the companies involved did not just build towns and then leave. They actively controlled those towns in ways that created serious human costs that are still felt today. Butte, Montana is probably the most instructive case. Butte sits on the Continental Divide in southwestern Montana at an elevation of about 5,500 ft. The mountain underneath it is [music] what geologists call a mineralized intrusive, which is a technical way of saying the rock is shot through with veins of ore in concentrations that are genuinely unusual even by the standards of the American [music] West. Initially, Butte was a silver town. Then, in the 1880s, the economics of copper changed everything. The electrification of American cities required copper wire in quantities that had never been needed before. Thomas Edison's electrical systems, the telegraph networks expanding across the continent, eventually the telephone. All of it ran on copper and Butte's mountain had copper in concentrations that made it, >> [music] >> in the common phrase of the era, the richest hill on Earth. The Anaconda [music] Copper Mining Company eventually came to control most of Butte's production. At its peak, Anaconda was producing roughly 1/3 of all the copper mined [music] in the United States. Butte's population reached close to 100,000 people. The company owned the mines, the smelter in the nearby town of Anaconda, the newspapers, the water utility, and significant portions of the commercial real estate. >> [music] >> The mines themselves were a vertical system of shafts and tunnels that eventually descended more than a mile underground. Miners worked in conditions that were, by any honest assessment, brutal. Heat increased with depth, approaching 120° Fahrenheit in the deeper levels. The rock dust caused silicosis, a lung disease that killed miners slowly over years. Cave-ins, fires, and gas explosions were regular occurrences. The worst single disaster in Butte mining history happened in June of 1917 when a fire broke out in the Granite [music] Mountain and Speculator mines. 163 miners died underground that day, most of them from carbon monoxide poisoning after the fire cut off their escape routes. That disaster happened in the same year as another event [music] that shows just how far company control could extend over a mining town. In Bisbee, Arizona 1917 the Phelps Dodge Corporation was dealing with a labor strike organized by the Industrial Workers of the World, also known as the Wobblies. The strike had shut down the copper mines there, and the company was not going to wait for a legal resolution. On the morning of July 12th, >> [music] >> 1917, the sheriff of Cochise County, working in coordination with Phelps Dodge officials, organized a group of more than 2,000 armed men, many of them company employees and local businessmen. Those men went door to door through Bisbee and rounded up anyone [music] connected to the strike. 1,286 men were loaded onto cattle [music] cars of the El Paso and Southwestern Railroad. They were transported across the desert to the town of Hermanas, New Mexico, [music] and left there in the desert with no food, no water, and no money. >> [music] >> This event, known as the Bisbee Deportation, was organized by a private corporation in coordination with local officials with no federal authorization and no legal process of any kind. President Woodrow Wilson called it a bad and illegal thing. A federal investigation agreed. Nobody was ever prosecuted. The men who were deported were not allowed to return to Bisbee for months. Many never came back at all. The copper mines at Bisbee continued operating until 1975, eventually producing over 8 billion pounds of copper from beneath the surrounding [music] hills. The pit that Phelps Dodge carved out of the landscape, the Lavender Pit, is a hole roughly 300 ft deep and half a mile across that sits right next to the surviving historic district of the town. Bisbee itself is one of the more intact former company towns in the American West because the historic buildings survived long enough to become a tourist attraction and eventually [music] an arts community. The company left, the town found a different reason to exist. Not every mining town was that lucky. Nevada alone has several hundred documented ghost [music] towns. Many of them the remnants of silver and gold booms from the late 1800s. Towns like Rhyolite, which had a population of around 10,000 in 1908 and was essentially empty by [music] 1912. Rhyolite had three-story banks, an ice cream parlor, and a rail connection. When the gold ran short and the investors pulled out, the town lasted about four years past its economic justification. The ruins of the Cook Bank building [music] in Rhyolite still stand in the Nevada desert. The concrete walls with their arched windows, minus the roof, visible from the road that runs through what used to be a street grid. There are historic interpretive signs now. A few tourists stop each year. That is what four years of boom and collapse looks like a century later. The pattern that produced these towns had a specific logic that is worth understanding because it did not happen by accident or through ignorance of what was coming. The companies that developed mining operations [music] in the American West were not run by naive optimists who genuinely believed the ore would last forever. They were run by sophisticated investors and engineers who had access to geological [music] surveys and production data. They knew, often decades in advance, that a given mine's productive life was limited. The company town model actually made the eventual abandonment [music] easier, not harder, from the corporation's perspective. If workers owned their homes, they would have equity to protect. They would have reasons to stay and fight for the town's future after the mine closed. They would have [music] political and economic leverage. But workers who rented from the company, [music] who were paid in script at the company store, who had no assets other than their labor, were fundamentally [music] portable in a way that asset-owning citizens were not. When the mine closed, the company could simply stop renting [music] the houses. Workers had no equity to lose because they had never been allowed to build any. They moved on to the next mining district, and the company moved on to developing it, replicating the same infrastructure model at the new location. This is why the American West [music] has so many ghost towns clustered around mine sites. The towns were not incidental [music] byproducts of mining. They were purpose-built instruments of labor management. Built fast, operated intensively, [music] and abandoned without sentiment when the economics stopped working. The human costs of this system were borne almost entirely by the workers and their families. A miner who spent 15 years in Butte or Creek [music] or Bisbee might have earned decent wages by the standards of the era, but he had no home equity, no pension, no long-term [music] stake in the place where he had spent the most productive years of his life. When the company left, he left, too, often with little more than he had arrived [music] with. His children had grown up in a company-owned school. His wife had shopped at a company-owned store. His social life had revolved [music] around institutions either directly owned or heavily influenced by the corporation. The company had, in effect, [music] substituted its own infrastructure for the civic infrastruc- -ture of an independent community. And when it left, that civic infrastructure left with it. The environmental costs followed a similar logic. The companies extracted value from the land and left the remediation costs behind. Butte is the starkest example of this. The Berkeley Pit, an open-pit copper mine carved into the same mountain that the [music] underground mines had worked for decades, was opened by the Anaconda Company in 1955. When Anaconda's suc- -cessor, Atlantic Richfield, shut down operations in 1982, they turned off the pumps that had been keeping groundwater out of the pit. The pit began filling with water that reacted with the sulfide minerals in the rock walls to become a highly acidic, heavy metal-laden lake. Today, the Berkeley Pit contains about 40 billion gallons of toxic water. The water level rises by about a foot each year. Federal regulators have established a critical water level above [music] which the contaminated water could begin flowing into the surrounding groundwater. The Superfund designation that covers Butte and the Silver Bow Creek watershed [music] is one of the largest in the country. The cleanup costs, which are still ongoing decades after the mine closed, run into the hundreds of millions of dollars. The company that made the profits from the mine paid a fraction of those costs. The rest fell on taxpayers. The people of Butte have lived with [music] that pit in their neighborhood for over 40 years since the mine closed. A flock of snow geese landed on the pit in 2016. [music] 265 of them died from exposure to the acidic water. This is not ancient history. This is happening now. The question that the story of American mining towns ultimately raises is whether the pattern was inevitable or whether it was a choice. The technology to mine ore at scale required capital investment that only large corporations could provide. That part is probably unavoidable given the era. You cannot build a mile-deep shaft system with small-scale operations. But the choice to house workers in company-owned rentals rather than encouraging home ownership was a policy decision, not a technical necessity. The choice to pay in script rather than currency was a choice. The choice to extract the resource, maximize profit during the productive years, and externalize [music] the cleanup costs onto future generations was a choice. A few towns tried to do it differently. Pueblo, Colorado, [music] which developed as a steel town rather than a pure mining town, managed to build [music] a more diversified economic base that allowed it to survive the decline of the steel industry, though not without serious pain. Leadville, Colorado, which went through multiple boom and bust cycles in silver and then lead and then molybdenum, eventually developed enough [music] civic infrastructure and enough independent ownership that it survived each collapse, shrunken but alive. Today, Leadville is the highest incorporated city in the United States, sitting at 10,152 feet elevation with a population of around 3,000, stubborn, high, cold, and still there. Most of the pure company towns were not that lucky because they were never designed to survive the company's departure. They were designed to serve the company while it was profitable. Survival after profitability was not part of the design specification. What is remarkable, looking back at all of this from a distance [music] of more than a century, is how thoroughly the physical evidence of these places survives. Drive through the mountains of Colorado or the desert valleys of Nevada and you will see them scattered across the landscape. Stone foundations where [music] buildings once stood, rusting headframes over mine shafts, mill foundations poured [music] in concrete that has survived a hundred winters, cemetery headstones for miners who died in caverns and fires and explosions. In some places, you can stand on a hillside and see the entire street grid of a town that [music] held 10,000 people now reduced to outlines in the ground. The streets are still there because dirt roads compacted by decades of foot traffic do not return to wilderness quickly. The lots are visible. You can walk the blocks. You can find the corner where the post office stood or the foundation of the hotel. A town is not just its buildings. It is the grid beneath the buildings and that grid can outlast the buildings by a very long time. >> [music] >> Rhyolite, Nevada, Bodie, California, St. Elmo Colorado Goldfield Nevada Virginia City, Montana, Silver City, Idaho. All of them ghost towns or near ghost towns now. All of them within living memory of their peak. Places where children went to school and women gave birth and men argued about city politics and speculators made fortunes and workers died in the dark underground. The mountain was what they came for. The mountain [music] was what drove them away when it was done with them. But the towns or what is left of them are still there, sitting in the wind and and snow and the high desert heat as if they are waiting [music] for something, as if they know the mountain still holds secrets that have not been pulled [music] out yet, which, in some of them, it does. If you want to see more videos exploring the forgotten corners of American history, go ahead and subscribe right now. Stories like this one are what this channel is about, [music] and there is a lot more where this came from. The mining town is, in the end, a compressed version of an argument that American society has been having with itself for a very long time, about who bears the costs of extraction, about whether a corporation that builds the infrastructure of a community incurs obligations to that community, about what it means to build something that you know, from the beginning, you intend to abandon. The men who built Creek and Butte and Bisbee were not villains in the cartoon sense. Many of them believed, or at least told themselves, that they were bringing [music] civilization to the wilderness. Roads electricity schools hospitals things that the frontier did not have, things that improved the lives of the people who came to work there. And in a narrow sense, they were right. The infrastructure was real, the wages were real, and in good years they were higher than a man could earn in most other industries. The communities that formed in these towns were real communities with real social bonds and real shared histories, but the structure underneath all of it, the ownership structure that kept workers permanently portable and permanently dependent, was what ensured that none of it would last, because things that are built to be abandoned get abandoned. Creek today has a casino economy that replaced the mining economy in the 1990s, when Colorado legalized limited gambling [music] in several historic mountain towns. The population is around 1200. The gold is still in the mountain, technically, but not in concentrations that are economic to mine at current prices. If gold prices spiked high enough, it might become [music] worth reopening. Companies have looked at it. Butte today is a city of around 34,000 people, down from its peak [music] of 100,000. The Berkeley Pit remains. The Superfund cleanup continues. [music] The historic Uptown district, with its Victorian commercial buildings, has been preserved >> [music] >> and is genuinely beautiful. The people who stayed, and there have always been people who [music] stayed, have built a community that is stubborn in the way that high altitude, cold weather, hard-used places tend to produce stubborn [music] people. Bisbee today has about 5,000 people. Most of them [music] artists and retirees who came for the architecture and the dry desert air. The old Phelps [music] Dodge headquarters building is still standing. The Lavender Pit is a tourist attraction. The deportees of 1917 are commemorated with a historical marker. The mountains are still there. They will be there when everything else about these stories has been forgotten. What they produced, for a few decades in the late 1800s and early 1900s, was something genuinely extraordinary. Cities in places where cities had no business [music] being. Infrastructure erected at altitude and in desert by men who came from the other side of the planet chasing the possibility of a better life. Mostly not finding it, but leaving something physical behind [music] regardless. Go stand at the edge of the Berkeley Pit some afternoon when the light is going orange over the mountains west of Butte. The water in the pit is a color that is somewhere between blue and green, depending on the angle and the season. It is, in a deeply strange way, beautiful. You can see the benches cut into the pit walls, the terraces where the shovels worked their way down through the rock. The whole thing is a wound in the mountain and a monument to what it costs to build a civilization out of what the ground holds. The mountain gave everything it had to give. The question that still does not have a clean answer is whether the people who came to pull it out were given a fair share of what that cost.

Đạo luật Homestead năm 1862 được cho là đưa những người nông dân nhỏ vào đất đai, và ở một số nơi nó đã làm được điều đó. Nhưng ở vùng núi Colorado, Nevada, Arizona và Montana, nghề nông là không phải đất đai tốt để làm gì. Những gì đất tốt cho là quặng. Vàng ở [âm nhạc] California đã chứng minh rằng một phát hiện duy nhất có thể lay chuyển hàng chục của hàng ngàn người trên khắp lục địa chỉ trong vài tháng. Nói ra rằng ngọn núi chứa đựng thứ gì đó có giá trị và dường như con người sẽ xuất hiện từ hư không để kéo giá trị đó ra khỏi mặt đất. Vấn đề là cơ sở hạ tầng. Một người đàn ông có thể đặt cược yêu cầu đặt cọc và tìm kiếm vàng trong một dòng suối với thiết bị trị giá vài đô la, nhưng loại quặng thực sự có giá trị, độ sâu những đường mạch vàng, bạc và đồng chạy xuyên qua tảng đá, được yêu cầu một cái gì đó khác biệt. segments.viText: Hãy đến đứng bên rìa Berkeley Pit vào một buổi chiều nào đó khi ánh sáng

segments.text: is going orange over the mountains west of Butte.
segments.viText: đang chuyển sang màu cam trên vùng núi phía tây Butte.

segments.text: The water in the pit is a color that is somewhere between blue and
segments.viText: Nước trong hố có màu nằm giữa màu xanh lam và

segments.text: green, depending on the angle and the season.
segments.viText: màu xanh lá cây, tùy theo góc độ và mùa.

segments.text: It is, in a deeply strange way, beautiful.
segments.viText: Nó đẹp một cách sâu sắc và kỳ lạ.

segments.text: You can see the benches cut into the pit walls, the terraces where the
segments.viText: Bạn có thể thấy những chiếc ghế dài cắt vào tường hố, sân thượng nơi

segments.text: shovels worked their way down through the rock.
segments.viText: những chiếc xẻng đang tìm đường xuyên qua tảng đá.

segments.text: The whole thing is a wound in the mountain and a monument to what
segments.viText: Toàn bộ sự việc là một vết thương trên núi và một tượng đài cho những gì

segments.text: it costs to build a civilization out of what the ground holds.
segments.viText: phải tốn kém để xây dựng một nền văn minh từ những gì đất đai nắm giữ.

segments.text: The mountain gave everything it had to give.
segments.viText: Ngọn núi đã cho đi tất cả những gì nó có thể cho đi.

segments.text: The question that still does not have a clean answer is whether the people
segments.viText: Câu hỏi vẫn chưa có câu trả lời rõ ràng là liệu con người

segments.text: who came to pull it out were given a fair share of what that
segments.viText: những người đến kéo nó ra sẽ được chia một phần công bằng những gì

segments.text: cost.
